content: 1. If you are not given the opportunity to meet with the Program Director or the person in charge, understand that this is often due to scheduling conflicts or the individual being too busy. Do not take it personally or assume it is intentional. Avoid letting this affect your attitude. Instead, remain confident and professional. Treat the Associate Program Director or whoever you meet with the same respect as you would the Program Director, as they often communicate directly with them. Do not ask the Program Coordinator or others why you did not meet the Program Director, as this can make you appear ungrateful or overly needy. 2. If you are asked to arrive later than other applicants, have fewer interviews, or are interviewed last, do not assume this is a reflection of your candidacy. It may simply be due to logistical reasons or poor coordination. Stay focused and confident. If you have fewer interviews, aim to make a strong impression in the time you have. If you are interviewed last, use it as an opportunity to leave a memorable final impression. 3. If you are left waiting for a long time, whether for an interview or lunch, remember that your behavior during this time is still being observed. Carry a small piece of candy if needed, but avoid chewing gum. Do not ask how much longer you will have to wait. Instead, use the time productively by reading about the program or engaging politely with other applicants. Avoid making jokes about the wait or hunger, as you never know who might overhear. 4. If you are forgotten about or get lost during the interview day, remain calm and proactive. Keep the department’s contact number with you in case you need to call and find out where others are. Do not take such situations personally or react with anger. 5. If you are asked inappropriate questions about race, religion, marital status, or other personal topics, stay composed and avoid reacting emotionally. If you are comfortable answering, do so, as the question may have been unintentional. If you prefer not to answer, pause and smile, giving the interviewer a chance to retract the question. If they do not, you can politely ask why they are asking or provide a vague response. Address any concerns about the question with the appropriate authorities after the interview, but avoid confrontation during the interview itself. 6. If you are asked to explain a deficiency in your record, acknowledge it honestly and take responsibility. Prepare in advance how you will address such questions. Stick to the facts, avoid making excuses or blaming others, and use “I” statements. Maintain a professional, objective, and humble demeanor. 7. If you feel inferior to other applicants or are compared to them by the interviewer, remind yourself that you were invited to interview, which already places you on an equal footing. Avoid asking other applicants about their scores or number of interviews, as this is impolite and can undermine your confidence. If an interviewer compares you to others, focus on your unique strengths and what you bring to the program. Stay composed and confident. 8. If the interviewer spends the entire time talking about themselves, use this as an opportunity to impress them. Be an active listener, show genuine interest, and ask thoughtful questions about what they are discussing. If you have researched the interviewer beforehand, bring up relevant points to engage them further. This approach can set you apart from other candidates who may have been disengaged or frustrated in similar situations. 9. If the interviewer invites you to ask questions, use this opportunity to demonstrate your interest and preparation. Ask thoughtful, program-specific questions that you have prepared in advance. Avoid generic or clichéd questions, as these can be saved for discussions with residents. Listen carefully to their answers and use them to formulate follow-up questions, creating a meaningful dialogue. 10. If the interviewer has not read your application, take the initiative to present yourself effectively. Prepare in advance to highlight your most positive and unique attributes succinctly. Use this as an opportunity to showcase your strengths without being constrained by any deficiencies in your record. Be proactive and incorporate key aspects of your application into the conversation. 11. If you are asked a tough clinical question, remain calm and take a moment to think before responding. If you know the answer, provide it confidently. If you do not know the answer, admit it honestly but explain how you would approach finding the correct information in a clinical setting. Avoid discussing the question with other applicants afterward or dwelling on how you could have answered differently. Focus on presenting yourself as a capable and resourceful candidate. 12. During a challenging interview experience, it is natural to feel frustrated or discouraged. However, it is important to remain professional and make the most of the opportunity. Avoid sabotaging the remainder of the day due to one negative experience. Stay positive, and focus on showcasing your strengths and learning about the program. You may find that, despite the challenges, the program is still a good fit for you.
